title: The Little Scientist: LLM Agent-Driven Discovery via the Scientific Method
summary:
What happens when you teach an LLM-based agent the scientific method?
  Motivation: Scientific discovery emerges from cycles of hypothesis, implementation, empirical testing, and feedback. Can this process be automated? We approach automated algorithm design through the lens of the scientific method, where an LLM-based agent goes through each step of the process in an ordered, iterative fashion.
  Results: We present The Little Scientist, a framework in which a "Scientist agent" works inside an evaluation environment that benchmarks its code and returns structured per-instance diagnostics. When the Scientist plateaus at a local optimum, a "Kuhn agent" injects a paradigm-shifting conjecture paired with a cross-disciplinary inspiration, forcing exploration of a different region of the LLM's latent space. We demonstrate the framework on two problems that require fundamentally different modes of discovery. For protein fitness prediction, the Scientist discovered Delta V, an ensemble calibration strategy that ranks first on the ProteinGym DMS Substitutions Zero-Shot leaderboard across all five official evaluation metrics, exceeding the #2 model (VenusREM) by +0.033 mean Spearman correlation across 217 DMS assays. For DNA motif discovery, the Scientist wrote an algorithm from scratch--DALE (Dual-seed Algorithm for Latent Enumeration)--that outperforms STREME (the default in the MEME Suite) across 132 ENCODE transcription factors (mean AUROC 0.842 vs. 0.803, Wilcoxon p < 10^{-6}) while running 11x faster. This demonstrates that the framework can produce genuinely novel algorithms, not just optimize existing components. Together, these results show that an LLM agent stepping through the scientific method can discover both new algorithms and new ensemble strategies that outperform prior solutions. The entire research program consumed 704M tokens on a single virtual machine with no GPUs

AI.tldr: The Little Scientist is a framework where an LLM-based agent applies the scientific method iteratively—hypothesizing, implementing, testing, and receiving structured feedback—to discover novel algorithms. It achieved state-of-the-art results in protein fitness prediction (Delta V) and DNA motif discovery (DALE), outperforming existing baselines while consuming 704M tokens on CPU-only infrastructure.
AI.motivation: The central question is whether the scientific discovery process—cycling through hypothesis, implementation, empirical testing, and feedback—can be automated by an LLM-based agent. The authors aim to move beyond simple optimization of existing components toward genuine discovery of novel algorithms.
AI.method: The framework consists of a "Scientist agent" that operates within an evaluation environment providing structured per-instance diagnostics. When the Scientist plateaus at a local optimum, a "Kuhn agent" injects a paradigm-shifting conjecture with cross-disciplinary inspiration to force exploration of new regions of the LLM's latent space.
AI.result: For protein fitness prediction, the discovered Delta V strategy ranks #1 on the ProteinGym DMS Substitutions Zero-Shot leaderboard across all five metrics. For DNA motif discovery, the DALE algorithm outperforms STREME on 132 ENCODE transcription factors (AUROC 0.842 vs 0.803) while running 11x faster. Uses 704M tokens on a single VM with no GPUs.
AI.conclusion: An LLM agent systematically following the scientific method can discover both new ensemble strategies and entirely new algorithms that outperform prior state-of-the-art solutions, demonstrating that LLM-based automated discovery is feasible and effective.

title: Dormancy stabilizes non-transitive competitive dynamics
summary: Competitive interactions can maintain diversity, yet coexistence is often fragile in well-mixed populations, where stochastic fluctuations can lead to extinction. This is the case in non-transitive systems, such as rock-paper-scissors dynamics, where no single type dominates globally. While spatial structure can stabilize these systems by providing refuges in space, it remains unclear whether analogous mechanisms can operate in time in well-mixed environments. Here, we develop a population-genetic framework showing that dormancy can act as a temporal refuge, preserving lineages and preventing collapse to fixation under interaction-driven fluctuations. We introduce a discrete-time Wright-Fisher model that combines generalized seed-banks with frequency-dependent interactions, allowing individuals to inherit their type from potential parents sampled across multiple past generations. This construction provides a tractable framework in which dormancy stores and later reintroduces lost types. In the case of either weak or moderate selection, we prove a multidimensional diffusion limit for the resulting type-frequency process and use it to analyze complex selective interactions. In non-transitive systems, dormancy stabilizes trajectories that would otherwise collapse through stochastic extinction, extends fixation times, and sustains coexistence. These effects cannot be explained solely by an increase in effective population size. Our results show that dormancy introduces temporal memory that qualitatively alters competitive dynamics, stabilizing otherwise fragile systems and enabling long-term coexistence.

AI.tldr: This paper develops a population-genetic framework showing that dormancy (seed-banks) can act as a temporal refuge in well-mixed populations, stabilizing non-transitive competitive systems like rock-paper-scissors dynamics by preserving lineages and preventing stochastic extinction, with a proven multidimensional diffusion limit demonstrating that temporal memory qualitatively alters competitive dynamics beyond simple effective population size effects.
AI.motivation: While spatial structure is known to stabilize non-transitive competitive systems by providing spatial refuges, it was unclear whether analogous refuge mechanisms could operate temporally in well-mixed environments where stochastic fluctuations often lead to collapse and extinction of coexistence.
AI.method: The authors develop a discrete-time Wright-Fisher model combining generalized seed-banks (dormancy) with frequency-dependent interactions, where individuals inherit their type from potential parents sampled across multiple past generations. They prove a multidimensional diffusion limit for the type-frequency process under weak or moderate selection and use this to analyze complex selective interactions.
AI.result: In non-transitive systems, dormancy stabilizes trajectories that would otherwise collapse through stochastic extinction, extends fixation times, and sustains coexistence. These stabilizing effects cannot be explained solely by an increase in effective population size.
AI.conclusion: Dormancy introduces temporal memory that qualitatively alters competitive dynamics, stabilizing otherwise fragile non-transitive systems and enabling long-term coexistence in well-mixed environments, thereby providing a temporal analog to spatial refuges.

title: scDNM-VAE enables directly inspectable deep clustering of single-cell RNA-seq data through signed dendritic gating
comment: 39 pages, 7 figures, 4 tables. Supplementary information available from the authors
summary:
Deep clustering models for single-cell RNA sequencing often assign cells through latent or centroid-based mechanisms that are difficult to inspect. We introduce scDNM-VAE (single-cell Dendritic Neuron Model Variational Autoencoder), a deep clustering framework that combines a variational autoencoder with a dendritic neuron-inspired head. Cluster assignments are governed by learnable signed synaptic weights and thresholds: the weight sign determines the direction of a gate's response to a latent coordinate, its magnitude controls steepness, and the weight-threshold pair determines the transition location. The trained clustering function can therefore be inspected directly without fitting a post-hoc explanation model.
  We benchmark scDNM-VAE on four datasets spanning immune, cortical, cardiac, and hematopoietic cells against scVI followed by KMeans and an MLP-DEC ablation. scDNM-VAE performs better than scVI on PBMC3k, comparably on the Human Heart Cell Atlas and Paul15, and worse on Zeisel, while producing biologically coherent marker-gene signatures. Ablating each cluster's three highest-magnitude synaptic dimensions causes numerically greater reassignment than random-dimension ablation across all datasets, but the margins are modest and negligible on Zeisel. These results show that signed dendritic gating supports competitive clustering with a parameter-inspectable decision function, while indicating that decision-relevant information is distributed across the latent space.

AI.tldr: scDNM-VAE is a deep clustering framework for single-cell RNA sequencing that combines a variational autoencoder with a dendritic neuron-inspired head, enabling directly inspectable cluster assignments governed by learnable signed synaptic weights and thresholds. It performs competitively against scVI on four benchmark datasets while offering interpretable decision functions.
AI.motivation: Existing deep clustering models for scRNA-seq data often rely on latent or centroid-based mechanisms that are difficult to inspect, making it hard to understand why cells are assigned to specific clusters.
AI.method: The framework integrates a VAE with a dendritic neuron-inspired head. Cluster assignments are controlled by learnable signed synaptic weights and thresholds, where weight sign determines gate response direction, magnitude controls steepness, and weight-threshold pairs determine transition locations, allowing direct inspection of the trained clustering function.
AI.result: Benchmarked on four datasets (immune, cortical, cardiac, hematopoietic cells), scDNM-VAE outperforms scVI on PBMC3k, performs comparably on Human Heart Cell Atlas and Paul15, and worse on Zeisel, while producing biologically coherent marker-gene signatures. Ablation of high-magnitude synaptic dimensions causes greater reassignment than random ablation across all datasets, though margins are modest.
AI.conclusion: Signed dendritic gating supports competitive clustering with a parameter-inspectable decision function, though decision-relevant information appears distributed across the latent space rather than concentrated in a few dimensions.

title: Leveraging generative hallucination and biophysics-informed modeling for unified biomolecular sequence-structure co-design
summary: Biomolecular design underpins applications from molecular recognition to therapeutics and synthetic biology, yet de novo interaction design remains challenging-especially for DNA/RNA, underexplored non-protein modalities with scarce, heterogeneous complex data and sharper geometric and chemical constraints. We introduce MCTH (Monte Carlo Tree Hallucination), an inference-only framework that casts all-atom sequence-structure co-design as uncertainty-aware planning over hallucinated states from pretrained folding and inverse-folding models, with optional biophysical control within the same decision loop. MCTH treats these models as frozen black-box operators and uses Monte Carlo Tree Search to allocate a fixed inference budget across competing design trajectories, incorporating model confidence and uncertainty, as well as cross-expert consensus/disagreement when multiple predictors are available. Across protein-RNA, protein-DNA, protein-protein, and protein-ligand design, matched-budget experiments show that adaptive search improves over simpler sampling and cycling strategies, while held-out AlphaFold3 and Chai-1 evaluations demonstrate transfer beyond the search-time oracle. MCTH provides a shared planning layer across modalities while allowing task-specific folding, inverse-folding, and biophysical modules, requiring no fine-tuning or backpropagation through component models.

AI.tldr: MCTH (Monte Carlo Tree Hallucination) is an inference-only framework for biomolecular sequence-structure co-design that uses Monte Carlo Tree Search to optimize design trajectories over frozen pretrained folding and inverse-folding models, with optional biophysical control. It performs adaptive budget allocation across design paths using model confidence, uncertainty, and cross-expert consensus, and demonstrates improvements over simpler sampling/cycling strategies across protein-RNA, protein-DNA, protein-protein, and protein-ligand tasks, with transfer validated on held-out AlphaFold3 and Chai-1.
AI.motivation: De novo biomolecular interaction design remains challenging, especially for non-protein modalities like DNA/RNA which have scarce, heterogeneous complex data and stricter geometric/chemical constraints. Existing approaches lack a unified framework that can handle diverse modalities and incorporate multiple predictive models without fine-tuning.
AI.method: MCTH casts all-atom sequence-structure co-design as uncertainty-aware planning over hallucinated states. It treats pretrained folding and inverse-folding models as frozen black-box operators and uses Monte Carlo Tree Search to allocate a fixed inference budget across competing design trajectories. The search incorporates model confidence, uncertainty, and cross-expert consensus/disagreement, with optional integration of biophysical control within the same decision loop. No fine-tuning or backpropagation through component models is required.
AI.result: Matched-budget experiments across protein-RNA, protein-DNA, protein-protein, and protein-ligand design show that adaptive MCTS search outperforms simpler sampling and cycling strategies. Held-out evaluations with AlphaFold3 and Chai-1 demonstrate that the results transfer beyond the search-time oracle used during optimization.
AI.conclusion: MCTH provides a shared, modality-agnostic planning layer for biomolecular design that can incorporate task-specific folding, inverse-folding, and biophysical modules, achieving state-of-the-art design performance without requiring model fine-tuning or end-to-end backpropagation.

title: DMT-Dens: Density-preserving manifold visualization for biological data
comment: 22 pages, 5 figures, 2 tables; includes supplementary material. Source code: https://github.com/Ruizhe-wang/DMT-Dens
summary: Motivation: Low-dimensional embeddings are widely used to explore cell-state heterogeneity in single-cell and other high-dimensional biological data. Although many methods preserve local neighborhoods, they may distort the apparent sampling density of processed observations, altering the visual contrast between dense and sparse regions and complicating the interpretation of rare, transitional, or continuous cell-state populations. Results: We present DMT-Dens, a parametric manifold-visualization method built on a latent-token Transformer encoder. The model integrates rank-based manifold alignment with hard-pair aggregation. To preserve density, it optimizes a loss based on the Pearson correlation between k-nearest-neighbor log-radius estimates in the processed input and two-dimensional embedding spaces. Benchmark evaluations demonstrate strong density preservation, particularly on biological datasets, while retaining competitive label separability. Availability: Source code, data-processing scripts, and resolved experiment configurations are available at https://github.com/Ruizhe-wang/DMT-Dens.

AI.tldr: DMT-Dens is a parametric manifold-visualization method using a latent-token Transformer encoder that preserves both local neighborhoods and sampling density in 2D embeddings by optimizing a Pearson correlation loss on k-NN log-radius estimates.
AI.motivation: Low-dimensional embeddings for single-cell data often distort apparent sampling density, altering visual contrast between dense and sparse regions and complicating interpretation of rare, transitional, or continuous cell states.
AI.method: DMT-Dens builds on a latent-token Transformer encoder with rank-based manifold alignment and hard-pair aggregation. It preserves density by optimizing a loss based on Pearson correlation between k-nearest-neighbor log-radius estimates in the input and 2D embedding spaces.
AI.result: Benchmark evaluations demonstrate strong density preservation, especially on biological datasets, while retaining competitive label separability.
AI.conclusion: DMT-Dens provides a parametric visualization approach that balances local structure preservation with accurate density representation, improving interpretation of rare and transitional cell populations. Source code and configurations are publicly available.

title: A Leakage-Proof Benchmark and Conformal Selective Triage for Electrohysterogram-Based Preterm Birth Prediction
comment: Accepted for publication in the Proceedings of the 48th Annual International Conference of the IEEE Engineering in Medicine and Biology Society (EMBC 2026), Toronto, Canada. Paper ID 4188
summary: Preterm birth remains a major cause of neonatal morbidity and mortality worldwide. Electrohysterography (EHG), a noninvasive measure of uterine myoelectrical activity, has been studied for preterm-birth prediction, but performance estimates may be biased when segments from the same maternal record are split across training and validation data. We formalized the distinction between segment-level and patient-independent record-grouped validation, established a patient-independent benchmark on the Term-Preterm Electrohysterogram Database, and evaluated class-conditional conformal selective prediction. All 300 records (38 preterm) were analyzed across three prespecified regimes. A 92-feature elastic-net logistic model was evaluated with record-grouped nested cross-validation; preprocessing, model fitting, Platt calibration, and conformal estimation were confined to training data, and performance was calculated from strictly out-of-fold record-level predictions with 1,000 bootstrap resamples. Under patient-independent evaluation, AUROC was 0.493 (95% CI 0.467-0.520), AUPRC 0.122 (0.095-0.152), and Brier score 0.115 (0.094-0.137). AUROC was 0.514 at or before 26 weeks and 0.469 thereafter. At miscoverage alpha=0.10, marginal coverage was 0.897, abstention 72.7%, and singleton-prediction accuracy 0.624. These findings establish a record-separated reference benchmark for EHG prediction and a broader validation principle for segmented physiological data: the unit of resampling should correspond to the unit at which predictive performance is intended to generalize. Conformal prediction further quantifies when the available information supports a singleton classification and when uncertainty warrants deferral.

AI.tldr: This study establishes a patient-independent benchmark for preterm-birth prediction using electrohysterography (EHG), showing that record-grouped validation yields near-chance performance (AUROC 0.493) and demonstrates the use of class-conditional conformal selective prediction to quantify when predictions should be deferred.
AI.motivation: Previous EHG-based preterm-birth prediction studies may have inflated performance estimates by splitting segments from the same maternal record across training and validation sets, violating patient independence. A rigorous, record-grouped benchmark is needed.
AI.method: All 300 records from the Term-Preterm Electrohysterogram Database (38 preterm) were analyzed. A 92-feature elastic-net logistic model was evaluated using record-grouped nested cross-validation, with preprocessing, model fitting, Platt calibration, and conformal estimation confined to training data. Performance was computed from strictly out-of-fold record-level predictions with 1,000 bootstrap resamples, and class-conditional conformal selective prediction was applied.
AI.result: Under patient-independent evaluation, AUROC was 0.493 (95% CI 0.467-0.520), AUPRC 0.122, and Brier score 0.115. AUROC was 0.514 at or before 26 weeks and 0.469 thereafter. At miscoverage alpha=0.10, marginal coverage was 0.897, abstention was 72.7%, and singleton-prediction accuracy was 0.624.
AI.conclusion: EHG features show near-chance patient-independent predictive performance for preterm birth in this dataset, establishing a record-separated reference benchmark. The key methodological principle is that the unit of resampling must correspond to the unit of intended generalization. Conformal prediction provides a principled mechanism for deferring predictions when uncertainty is high.

title: Recovering protein conformations from single-particle cryo-EM data via indirect shape matching gradient flows
summary: Single-particle cryo-electron microscopy images a macromolecule as many noisy tomographic projections of its electrostatic potential. We reconstruct the protein backbone directly from such projections, as an atomic point cloud, without the intermediate step of reconstructing the 3D electrostatic potential map. We formulate this as an indirect shape matching problem: a point-cloud template of the backbone is deformed until its simulated projections agree with the data, with the structure observed only through the imaging operator. The deformation is computed via a gradient flow on a Lie group, and we derive the resulting framework in a general geometric setting before adapting it for single-particle cryo-electron microscopy. On synthetic data, we recover single- and multichain proteins and capture conformational transitions.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a novel approach for reconstructing protein backbones directly from single-particle cryo-EM projections as atomic point clouds, bypassing the conventional intermediate step of 3D electrostatic potential map reconstruction. The method formulates this as an indirect shape matching problem with a gradient flow on a Lie group, demonstrated on synthetic data for single- and multichain proteins and conformational transitions.
AI.motivation: Traditional cryo-EM reconstruction requires an intermediate step of reconstructing the 3D electrostatic potential map before building atomic models. This paper aims to bypass this bottleneck by directly reconstructing protein backbones from noisy projections, potentially improving efficiency and accuracy.
AI.method: The approach formulates backbone reconstruction as an indirect shape matching problem: a point-cloud template of the protein backbone is deformed until its simulated projections match the observed cryo-EM data. Since the structure is observed only through the imaging operator, the deformation is computed via a gradient flow on a Lie group, derived in a general geometric setting and then adapted for single-particle cryo-EM.
AI.result: On synthetic data, the method successfully recovers single-chain and multichain proteins, and can capture conformational transitions.
AI.conclusion: Direct backbone reconstruction from cryo-EM projections is feasible without explicit 3D map reconstruction, offering a potentially streamlined approach to structure determination.

title: Mathematical modelling of immune persistence and relapse pathways in CAR T-cell therapy for B-ALL
summary: Chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T-cell therapy has transformed the treatment of B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukaemia (B-ALL). Despite high initial response rates, a substantial fraction of patients relapse, often due to loss of CAR T-cell persistence, antigen escape, or immune-privileged sites that shield tumour cells. Prolonged CAR T-cell persistence is clinically associated with durable remission, but why it is required remains poorly understood. To address this, we develop and analyse the BEAM (Blast, Effector, Activated, Memory) model of CAR T-cell dynamics in B-ALL. BEAM extends predator--prey models with three CAR T-cell states (memory, activated, effector) coupled to a logistic growth equation for the blasts, calibrated against the FELIX trial of obecabtagene autoleucel in adult B-ALL. We find that both memory and effector persistence prevent relapse, but for distinct reasons: memory persistence sustains surveillance against low-burden or slowly proliferating residual disease, while effector persistence clears isolated blasts emerging from immune-privileged sites. The model further predicts a trade-off between immediate cytotoxicity and durable surveillance, and identifies initial tumour burden as a key modifiable factor for reducing antigen-negative relapse. Together, these results offer a framework for designing more durable, individually tailored CAR T-cell therapies.

AI.tldr: The paper presents BEAM, a mathematical model of CAR T-cell dynamics in B-ALL that extends predator-prey models with three T-cell states (memory, activated, effector) coupled to logistic blast growth, calibrated against the FELIX trial. The model shows that memory and effector persistence prevent relapse through distinct mechanisms and predicts a trade-off between immediate cytotoxicity and durable surveillance.
AI.motivation: Despite high initial response rates in CAR T-cell therapy for B-ALL, many patients relapse due to poor CAR T-cell persistence, antigen escape, or immune-privileged sites. Prolonged CAR T-cell persistence is clinically linked to durable remission, but the mechanistic reasons for why persistence is required remain poorly understood.
AI.method: Developed the BEAM (Blast, Effector, Activated, Memory) model, extending predator-prey models with three CAR T-cell states coupled to a logistic growth equation for leukemic blasts. The model was calibrated against clinical data from the FELIX trial of obecabtagene autoleucel in adult B-ALL.
AI.result: Both memory and effector persistence prevent relapse but through distinct mechanisms: memory persistence sustains surveillance against low-burden/slowly proliferating residual disease, while effector persistence clears isolated blasts emerging from immune-privileged sites. The model also predicts a trade-off between immediate cytotoxicity and durable surveillance, and identifies initial tumour burden as a key modifiable factor for reducing antigen-negative relapse.
AI.conclusion: The BEAM model provides a framework for understanding CAR T-cell persistence mechanisms and offers insights for designing more durable, individually tailored CAR T-cell therapies.

title: Grounding Healthcare LLMs in a Causal Knowledge Graph: Framework, Metrics, and a Cardiovascular Pilot
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly proposed for healthcare decision support, but their evaluations still reward single-answer accuracy rather than reasoning about interventions, mechanisms, harms, evidence, and uncertainty. We propose a reproducible, graph-centered evaluation framework for intervention-oriented LLM behavior in healthcare and stress-test it in a cardiovascular pilot. The framework has four components: (i) a domain causal knowledge graph in which assertions are first-class, provenance-preserving nodes with stable identifiers; (ii) a scenario-conditioned subgraph extraction step that, given any clinical scenario, retrieves the relevant reified-assertion subgraph; (iii) four controlled grounding conditions that vary how the retrieved subgraph is composed into the model's context (ungrounded C1, knowledge-graph C2, causal-graph C3, integrated C4); and (iv) an automated scoring pipeline, anchored on assertion identifiers, that computes intervention accuracy, and other evaluation measures on a single pass. To test the framework, we built a category-balanced scenario generator across eight reasoning failure modes and instantiated it on a cardiovascular graph. The metric panel discriminates conditions along interpretable, non-redundant axes: C4 obtains the strongest causal edge F1 (0.838), adverse-effect F1 (0.833), evidence accuracy (0.738), and unsupported claim rate (0.114), while C1 obtains the highest raw intervention accuracy (0.948) with no measurable causal or evidential grounding.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a graph-centered evaluation framework for assessing intervention-oriented reasoning of LLMs in healthcare, using a causal knowledge graph with provenance-preserving assertion nodes, scenario-conditioned subgraph extraction, four controlled grounding conditions, and an automated scoring pipeline. A cardiovascular pilot demonstrates that the framework discriminates across interpretable axes—the fully integrated condition (C4) achieves the best causal reasoning and evidence metrics, while ungrounded LLMs (C1) achieve high raw accuracy without causal or evidential grounding.
AI.motivation: Current LLM evaluations in healthcare reward single-answer accuracy rather than assessing deeper reasoning about interventions, mechanisms, harms, evidence, and uncertainty—dimensions that are critical for trustworthy clinical decision support.
AI.method: A four-component framework: (i) a domain causal knowledge graph with reified assertions as first-class, provenance-preserving nodes having stable identifiers; (ii) scenario-conditioned subgraph extraction; (iii) four grounding conditions (ungrounded C1, knowledge-graph C2, causal-graph C3, integrated C4); and (iv) an automated scoring pipeline computing intervention accuracy and other measures anchored on assertion identifiers. A category-balanced scenario generator across eight reasoning failure modes was built and tested on a cardiovascular graph.
AI.result: The metric panel discriminates conditions along interpretable, non-redundant axes. C4 achieved the strongest causal edge F1 (0.838), adverse-effect F1 (0.833), evidence accuracy (0.738), and lowest unsupported claim rate (0.114), while C1 achieved the highest raw intervention accuracy (0.948) but with no measurable causal or evidential grounding.
AI.conclusion: A graph-centered, assertion-anchored evaluation framework can reveal meaningful trade-offs in LLM healthcare reasoning—showing that high raw accuracy does not imply causal soundness or evidential grounding, and that integrated grounding improves clinically critical reasoning dimensions.

title: Phase-based spatial ordinal patterns for characterizing oscillatory dynamics
summary: The emergence of organized spatiotemporal patterns is ubiquitous in oscillatory systems, from neural populations to engineered networks. Identifying these patterns and tracking how they evolve over time remains challenging, particularly when systems exhibit transient dynamics. Here, we introduce a framework based on spatial ordinal patterns to characterize the spatiotemporal dynamics of oscillatory systems. Our approach acts directly on the phase rather than the amplitude, with additional patterns introduced to account for near-equal phases. This symbolic representation encodes local spatial ordering relations, capturing both phase gradients and synchronized clusters within a single framework. From this construction, we define a spatial permutation entropy that quantifies the diversity of spatiotemporal patterns at each point in time, enabling the detection of transient dynamics and regime transitions as they occur. We show that this approach distinguishes phase-locked states with identical levels of global synchronization but distinct spatial organization and also characterizes partially synchronized states. We demonstrate the method on synthetic oscillator networks across multiple spatiotemporal regimes, and on resting-state EEG recordings from human volunteers, where it distinguishes different conditions within individual volunteers.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a framework based on spatial ordinal patterns to characterize spatiotemporal dynamics in oscillatory systems. By encoding local spatial phase ordering relations into symbolic representations, it defines a spatial permutation entropy that quantifies pattern diversity over time, enabling detection of transient dynamics and regime transitions. The method distinguishes phase-locked states with identical synchronization levels but different spatial organization, and is validated on synthetic oscillator networks and resting-state EEG recordings.
AI.motivation: Identifying and tracking organized spatiotemporal patterns in oscillatory systems remains challenging, particularly when systems exhibit transient dynamics. Existing approaches struggle to capture both phase gradients and synchronized clusters within a single framework while detecting regime transitions in real time.
AI.method: The framework operates on phase (not amplitude) using spatial ordinal patterns that encode local spatial ordering relations. Additional patterns are introduced to handle near-equal phases. From this symbolic representation, a spatial permutation entropy is defined to quantify the diversity of spatiotemporal patterns at each time point, enabling detection of transient dynamics and regime transitions as they occur.
AI.result: The approach distinguishes phase-locked states with identical global synchronization levels but distinct spatial organization, characterizes partially synchronized states, and is demonstrated on synthetic oscillator networks across multiple spatiotemporal regimes. Validation on resting-state EEG recordings from human volunteers shows the method distinguishes different conditions within individual volunteers.
AI.conclusion: The proposed spatial ordinal pattern framework provides a unified symbolic representation that captures both phase gradients and synchronized clusters, with spatial permutation entropy serving as an effective real-time measure for detecting transient dynamics and regime transitions in oscillatory systems.

title: Empirical mode decomposition and interpretable machine learning for preterm birth classification from electrohysterography
comment: 33 pages, 9 figures. Submitted to PLOS ONE. Umesha Tilakarathna and Senith Jayakody contributed equally to this work
summary: Preterm birth (PTB) remains a major global health problem, and reliable non-invasive risk assessment remains difficult. Electrohysterography (EHG) records uterine electrical activity from the maternal abdomen and may support PTB assessment, but performance can be inflated when segments from the same recording are split across training and validation folds. We evaluated empirical mode decomposition (EMD) for term-versus-preterm classification using 26 pregnancy recordings (13 preterm, 13 term) from the public TPEHGT dataset. Annotated intervals and non-overlapping fixed 3-minute windows were compared, and the first four intrinsic mode functions (IMFs) were evaluated. Fourteen features from each of three EHG channels were assessed with nine classifiers using repeated five-fold recording-grouped cross-validation and recording-level aggregation. IMF1 gave the strongest mean performance. With fixed 3-minute IMF1 features, Random Forest achieved mean accuracy 0.8308, F1 0.7969, balanced accuracy 0.8308, MCC 0.6998, ROC-AUC 0.8157, and average precision 0.8877. IMF1 also outperformed matched filtered time-domain features across all reported mean metrics. Preterm recordings showed smaller, more regularly spaced peak-like events, lower temporal-energy measures, and higher entropy. These findings support further evaluation of IMF1-based EHG classification in larger independent cohorts.

AI.tldr: This study evaluates empirical mode decomposition (EMD) for preterm birth classification using electrohysterography (EHG) recordings from the TPEHGT dataset. Using recording-grouped cross-validation to prevent data leakage, IMF1 features with Random Forest achieved the strongest performance (accuracy 0.83, ROC-AUC 0.82), outperforming filtered time-domain features.
AI.motivation: Preterm birth remains a major global health problem, and reliable non-invasive risk assessment is difficult. EHG may support PTB assessment, but prior performance can be inflated when segments from the same recording are split across training and validation folds, necessitating a rigorous evaluation with recording-grouped cross-validation.
AI.method: Using 26 pregnancy recordings (13 preterm, 13 term) from TPEHGT dataset, the study applied empirical mode decomposition (EMD) to extract the first four intrinsic mode functions (IMFs). Fourteen features from each of three EHG channels were assessed with nine classifiers using repeated five-fold recording-grouped cross-validation and recording-level aggregation. Annotated intervals and non-overlapping fixed 3-minute windows were compared.
AI.result: IMF1 gave the strongest mean performance. With fixed 3-minute IMF1 features, Random Forest achieved mean accuracy 0.8308, F1 0.7969, balanced accuracy 0.8308, MCC 0.6998, ROC-AUC 0.8157, and average precision 0.8877. IMF1 outperformed matched filtered time-domain features. Preterm recordings showed smaller, more regularly spaced peak-like events, lower temporal-energy measures, and higher entropy.
AI.conclusion: The findings support further evaluation of IMF1-based EHG classification in larger independent cohorts, suggesting that EMD-based feature extraction provides a promising and methodologically rigorous approach for non-invasive preterm birth risk assessment.

title: An information-theoretic perspective on feed-forward loop abundances in transcriptional networks
summary: Biological networks feature recurring motifs, but their uneven abundance remains poorly understood. Feed-forward loops (FFLs) are important motifs in the transcriptional networks of \textit{Escherichia coli} and \textit{Saccharomyces cerevisiae}, yet their eight types appear in highly unequal frequencies. This study presents an information-theoretic framework that decomposes input-output mutual information into pathway and interference components. The interference mutual information (IMI) quantifies the joint influence of direct and indirect regulatory pathways on information transmission. Our results show that IMI closely follows the observed abundance patterns in both organisms, whereas the input-output mutual information and the pathway component do not. We also trace the IMI hierarchy to the strength of pathway-interference interactions and local pathway sensitivities. Notably, a stronger IMI is also associated with reduced robustness to parameter variation, suggesting a trade-off between information processing and resilience in gene regulatory circuits. Our results, thus, identify a topology-dependent information-theoretic feature that relates to the abundance patterns.

AI.tldr: This paper presents an information-theoretic framework decomposing mutual information into pathway and interference components to explain the uneven abundance of feed-forward loop (FFL) types in E. coli and S. cerevisiae transcriptional networks. The interference mutual information (IMI) closely matches observed FFL abundance patterns, while other information measures do not, and stronger IMI correlates with reduced parameter robustness, suggesting a trade-off between information processing and resilience.
AI.motivation: Biological networks exhibit recurring feed-forward loop motifs whose eight types appear in highly unequal frequencies, yet the reasons for this uneven abundance remain poorly understood. The authors aim to identify a topology-dependent information-theoretic feature that can explain these observed abundance patterns.
AI.method: An information-theoretic framework decomposes input-output mutual information into pathway and interference components. The interference mutual information (IMI) quantifies the joint influence of direct and indirect regulatory pathways on information transmission, and its relationship to FFL abundance is examined across E. coli and S. cerevisiae. The IMI hierarchy is traced to pathway-interference interaction strengths and local pathway sensitivities.
AI.result: IMI closely follows the observed FFL abundance patterns in both organisms, whereas input-output mutual information and pathway components do not. Stronger IMI is associated with reduced robustness to parameter variation, indicating a trade-off between information processing and resilience.
AI.conclusion: The study identifies IMI as a topology-dependent information-theoretic feature that correlates with FFL abundance patterns, suggesting that interference between regulatory pathways may drive motif selection in evolved gene regulatory circuits, with an inherent trade-off between information processing capability and robustness.
